newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia growth rises but price pressures up.
newsitem.headline: Russia growth rises but price pressures up.

text.p: Russian gross domestic product leapt in August and unemployment edged down, but a big rise in wholesale prices pointed to a build-up of inflationary pressures, official figures released on Friday showed.

GDP rose five percent in August, the biggest monthly rise for over a year, the State Statistics Committee said. But because of sharp falls at the start of 1996, it was still eight percent lower than a year earlier.
Industrial prices, the prices charged by factories to their customers, rose 2.1 percent in August after 1.2 percent in July.
Economists said the rise in output was good news, although it was too soon to say whether it marked a new trend.
The rise in wholesale prices was not unduly alarming, as consumer price inflation seems under control.
But tax problems, with revenue well below budgeted levels inflating the budget deficit, could stifle any recovery.

"The fact that GDP and industrial output look like they're in better shape than in the last months is positive, but I would wonder if that's going to be sustainable if the government places more stringent demands on companies," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Jim Nail.
"We're not out of the woods yet."
Peter Boone of the London School of Economics told a news conference the government could finance the deficit by non-inflationary means by issuing Treasury bills.

"It is a problem in that it will hurt the recovery," said Boone. "It means the government will take funds from financial markets and spend them and those funds could be otherwise used for investments."
The deficit is the bleak side of Russia's economic picture, while sharply lower inflation rates give grounds for optimism.
Consumer prices actually fell 0.2 percent in August, and have risen only 16.1 percent so far this year, compared with 96 percent in the first eight months of 1995.
News that commercial bank creditors had agreed in principal to reschedule $35 billion of debts Russia inherited from former Soviet Union could also be positive.

The International Monetary Fund, which is backing Russian reforms with a $10 billion loan, delayed the July monthly payment of the credit because of concern on how low revenues would hit the deficit. It has now paid the July tranche and was likely to decide on the August instalment later on Friday.

Russian officials had hoped the economy, which is now less than two thirds of its size in 1991, would start to recover this year. But they recently acknowledged that GDP will not grow until 1997 at the earliest.

Economists say official data probably understate the strength of the economy as they fail to measure adequately the activities of newly created small companies -- many of which are bent on hiding from the taxman.
A small fall in unemployment to 6.68 million, or 9.2 percent of the workforce, from 6.73 million in July, the first fall for over a year, could also indicate the start of a recovery.
United City Bank economist Christopher Granville said 1996 would turn out to be another year of recession although some sectors such as forest goods were already recovering well.
"We're going to probably end the year with another fall in recorded GDP, but that's not going to mean anything in itself. The timing of growth has slipped a bit," he said.
Granville said the key to getting the economy moving was a sustained fall in interest rates.
But inflation is now so subdued that the rise in wholesale prices was not immediately a threat, even though other price rises, such as electricity rates, are in the pipeline.
